children: As the world's leading authority on all things leather, having publicly confessed to spending $600,000 on leather jackets, pants and boots, it is only fitting that I pass final judgment on the sartorial choices of Jensen Huang.

The entire world knows at this point that the beleaguered former CEO of Nvidia fancies leather jackets, the media obsession such that Huang's style has become almost as noteworthy as an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy. It has unleashed the verbal nonsense of the cultural critics who find leather a dangerous taboo with all sorts of connotations beyond the actual wearing of it. By donning a leather jacket, Huang has been accused of committing an unforgivable haberdashery faux pas. Among the sentiments — he is far too old to be wearing leather, a midlife crisis right up there with a red sports car; he is trying to look cool when it is physically impossible for a tech dweeb to look cool.

Huang likes leather. He looks good in a jacket and even if he did not, that's his personal choice. Does he feel a certain sexual twinge when he puts one on — the tightness of the sleeves, the aphrodisia of the scent, the smooth texture? God I hope so. Does he look into the mirror and do a little pirouette and start humming "Welcome to the Jungle?" God I hope so. Much has been made of the fact he owns 30 to 40 leather jackets. It might seem excessive unless you are a leather fetishist. Then it's child's play. At my peak, I owned over a hundred jackets, along with dozens of pairs of pants and boots and gloves. It became a compulsive addiction, and although I finally licked it, I miss the rush of the UPS man coming to the front door everyday with half a dozen packages and wondering what the hell was going on.

I also miss the $600,000 I spent, some of the purchases so impulsive they did not even fit. Was I going through a midlife crisis? All of life is a crisis, and whatever you can do at any age to feel better about yourself is a wonderful thing. And for the record I did try a sports car, which did not work despite leather seats.

Huang did not go far enough; his jackets pretty much look the same, not tight enough, not sexy enough. He is also extremely rich and when you are extremely rich, you do stupidly rich things, like fancy a Tom Ford model for $9,000 when the only reason you buy Tom Ford is because you can buy Tom Ford and want everyone to know you have Tom Ford — even though you can buy a jacket that looks pretty much the same for one-tenth of the price.

Even with a purge, which occurred right after I got out of rehab for addiction and compulsive disorder, I still own over 40 leather jackets. I have leather from every major designer — Gucci, YSL, Philipp Plein, Jitrois, Schott, Belstaff. They are my precious babies with lives all their own and there is an urge to tuck them in at night.

I love wearing full leather and in keeping with the image, I learned to ride a motorcycle at the age of 60 where the wearing of leather is obligatory. I like the rocker look at the age of 72 when the only rocker I should be thinking about is a rocking chair.

You may think this is excessive, but there are some leather disciples out there who wear elbow length black leather gloves 24 hours a day — when they sleep, when they eat, even when they type. That's too much even for me: I only wear them to bed several times a month.
There were stares at first when I came out in public. There still are, almost all of them from sadly repressed white males whose idea of fashion is wearing loafers without socks.
Do I wonder how much longer I can pull it off given my age? Of course. Am I trying to be someone I'm not? Of course.
So let Jensen Huang have his leather jacket.
I'm pretty sure he has more important things to worry about anyway, such as disgrace, humiliation, embarrassment and possible criminality.
